events.title: Rider Advocate brief: 6 claims (0 void)
events.body:
C1: The GPS record shows the driver drove one off-route segment from 12:46 to 13:07 covering 9.70 km where the optimal route covers only 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km, and never returning to the shortest path (up to 1720 m off the optimal route) — an unexempted deviation. [F3 F1] [RD-1]
C2: No justification exists for the deviation: there were no traffic incidents recorded near the route during the trip window, all expressway speed bands were free-flowing (60–69 km/h), and the weather was fair with no rain; the only slow band was on Paya Lebar Road, which is not on the alternative the driver claims the GPS chose. [F12 F9 F10 F11 F13] [RD-4]
C3: No consent was given for any route change: there were no in-app chat messages between rider and driver, so no rider message precedes the 12:46 segment start; the driver's own statement is a post-trip narrative about following his GPS, not an assertion of a rider-agreed route, and a driver's account cannot substitute for the rider's own consent message. [F7 F8] [RD-5]
C4: Because this is a metered RydeTAXI trip, the deviation entered the fare directly: the fare facts bill the excess 4.61 km at $1.4099/km = $6.50, and the total charged was $42.52 with distance fare $28.31 on 20.08 km. [F4 F6] [RD-2]
C5: Refund is therefore $4.08 × ($28.31 ÷ 20.08 km = $1.4099/km) = $5.75 for the unexempted segment alone; the remaining 0.52–0.53 km difference between the billed excess (4.61 km) and the segment sum (4.08 km) is map-matching/route-corridor mileage not attributable to any segment and is not claimed. [F3 F4 F6] [RD-2]
C6: This is a repeated breach: the rider's profile records 3 route disputes already upheld against drivers in the last 90 days and the driver's profile shows 1 prior dispute with 0 upheld, so the driver's account warrants Ryde account review alongside the refund. [F14 F15] [RD-6]
Weaknesses: The rider's profile shows 5 disputes in 90 days (3 upheld) (F14), which the other side may use to argue the rider disputes fares habitually and to dilute the weight of this complaint. | The driver has 640 trips in 90 days, a 4.8 rating and 0 upheld route disputes (F15); the judge may treat the deviation as an isolated navigation error rather than a pattern — although our RD-6 request only asks for account review, not a finding of 'repeated' against this driver. | The driver's statement (F8) claims his GPS routed him off at Paya Lebar; no fact in the record ties the 12:46–13:07 segment to any named road, and if the judge reads the driver as having a 'reasonable cause' explanation the segment could be found exempt — though RD-4 requires traffic evidence, which F12 shows is absent. | Claim C5's $5.75 rests on the fact-table per-km rate ($1.4099, derived from F4/F6) rather than Ryde's published taxi unit rate (policy gap G10), so the exact figure could be recalculated slightly differently. | We claim only the segment's 4.08 km and not the full billed excess of 4.61 km (F4), so a smaller sum than the rider expected is requested.
Asks: refund_partial $5.75

claims.assertion: The GPS record shows the driver drove one off-route segment from 12:46 to 13:07 covering 9.70 km where the optimal route covers only 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km, and never returning to the shortest path (up to 1720 m off the optimal route) — an unexempted deviation.

No justification exists for the deviation: there were no traffic incidents recorded near the route during the trip window, all expressway speed bands were free-flowing (60–69 km/h), and the weather was fair with no rain; the only slow band was on Paya Lebar Road, which is not on the alternative the driver claims the GPS chose.

No consent was given for any route change: there were no in-app chat messages between rider and driver, so no rider message precedes the 12:46 segment start; the driver's own statement is a post-trip narrative about following his GPS, not an assertion of a rider-agreed route, and a driver's account cannot substitute for the rider's own consent message.

Because this is a metered RydeTAXI trip, the deviation entered the fare directly: the fare facts bill the excess 4.61 km at $1.4099/km = $6.50, and the total charged was $42.52 with distance fare $28.31 on 20.08 km.

Refund is therefore $4.08 × ($28.31 ÷ 20.08 km = $1.4099/km) = $5.75 for the unexempted segment alone; the remaining 0.52–0.53 km difference between the billed excess (4.61 km) and the segment sum (4.08 km) is map-matching/route-corridor mileage not attributable to any segment and is not claimed.

This is a repeated breach: the rider's profile records 3 route disputes already upheld against drivers in the last 90 days and the driver's profile shows 1 prior dispute with 0 upheld, so the driver's account warrants Ryde account review alongside the refund.

weaknesses: The rider's profile shows 5 disputes in 90 days (3 upheld) (F14), which the other side may use to argue the rider disputes fares habitually and to dilute the weight of this complaint.

The driver has 640 trips in 90 days, a 4.8 rating and 0 upheld route disputes (F15); the judge may treat the deviation as an isolated navigation error rather than a pattern — although our RD-6 request only asks for account review, not a finding of 'repeated' against this driver.

The driver's statement (F8) claims his GPS routed him off at Paya Lebar; no fact in the record ties the 12:46–13:07 segment to any named road, and if the judge reads the driver as having a 'reasonable cause' explanation the segment could be found exempt — though RD-4 requires traffic evidence, which F12 shows is absent.

Claim C5's $5.75 rests on the fact-table per-km rate ($1.4099, derived from F4/F6) rather than Ryde's published taxi unit rate (policy gap G10), so the exact figure could be recalculated slightly differently.
We claim only the segment's 4.08 km and not the full billed excess of 4.61 km (F4), so a smaller sum than the rider expected is requested.

D8: Because the off-route segment is unexcused, the metered overcharge falls to be refunded, but only the distance units of the unexcused segment to the exclusion of corridor/matching distance, i.e. not the full $6.50; the segment's 4.08 km x $1.4099/km = $5.75 (rounded to the cent) (F3, F4). events.title: Proposed ruling: refund_partial $5.75 (model confidence 0.90)
events.body:
This is a metered RydeTAXI trip, so a route deviation feeds directly into the fare; the trip ran Clarke Quay → Bedok Mall with an optimal route of 15.5 km while 20.1 km was driven, and the trace marks one off-route segment 12:46–13:07 covering 9.70 km where the optimal route covers 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km [F1][F3][RD-1]. No exemption applies to that segment: no traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window, and the only band evidence is free-flowing speed bands 7 on the CTE/PIE plus band 4 on Paya Lebar Road, which never reaches bands 1–2 and in any case cannot exempt a segment alone [F9][F10][F11][F12][RD-4].

Consent under RD-5 also fails. The record contains no in-app chat at all, so no rider message sent before the 12:46 segment start could agree to any route change, and the driver's post-trip statement that he "followed my GPS" is a statement, not rider consent [F7][F8][RD-5]. The same emptiness of the chat record means there was no rider-named stop, so RD-3 gives no relief either [F7][F3][RD-3]. The segment therefore counts as unexempted and is refundable under RD-2.

Amount: the fare fact gives this trip's per-km rate as distance fare ÷ distance km = $28.31 ÷ 20.08 km = $1.4099/km [F6][F4][RD-2]. Applying it to the unexempted segment's extra distance: 4.08 km × $1.4099/km = $5.7524, i.e. $5.75. The residual difference between the extra km of the segment (4.08 km) and the billed excess distance (4.61 km) is route-corridor / map-matching movement not attributed to any segment and is not refundable [F4][F6][RD-2].

Flag: the driver's profile shows 0 route disputes upheld in the last 90 days, so the condition for a repeated-breach account flag is not met on the driver's account [F15][RD-6]; no account action is issued.

✗ RD-4 (a) incident on the replaced stretch, reported before the detour [F3] no qualifying incident (speed band alone does not exempt) (no evidence)

? RD-5 rider agreed to this route before the detour; scope of that agreement [F3] RULE: exempt only if a RIDER message sent before 12:46:55 agrees AND the agreement covers this segment. Three kinds of agreement: (1) GENERAL route choice ('take whichever way is faster') covers a route chosen to get there, not an errand of the driver's own (a stop away from the route, a loop that reaches nothing: counts). (2) A SPECIFIC named road or area ('go round via X') covers driving on X only: the record must tie this segment to X (a stop on X, a message placing the car on X, a road name in a fact); timing alone does not, and the fact table carries no road names for the driven path — if nothing ties them, the finding is undetermined (G13); if the record places this segment somewhere else (a stop away from X, the driver's own statement naming another road or place, a stop the driver chose the location of), the agreement to X does not cover it: counts. (3) Scope unclear: undetermined. A driver's claim of agreement that appears only in his statement is not consent (G11); a complete chat record with no rider agreement before the segment: counts. This finding changes the amount. Evidence — F8: Driver statement (written after the trip, not part of the chat): “I followed my GPS, it took me off at Paya Lebar. Nothing wrong with the fare.” (F8)

A stop the rider asked for without naming a place ('a 7-Eleven on the way') does not excuse the driver's choice of a far one → counts. No stop measured in this segment. (no evidence)

what_would_change: F3: the judge found no rider agreement covering this segment, so $5.75 is refunded; a rider message agreeing to it before it started would have exempted it.
Had the driver carried a prior upheld route dispute in the last 90 days, RD-6 would add an account flag.

claims.assertion: The GPS record shows the driver drove one off-route segment from 12:46 to 13:07 covering 9.70 km where the optimal route covers only 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km, and never returning to the shortest path (up to 1720 m off the optimal route) — an unexempted deviation.

No justification exists for the deviation: there were no traffic incidents recorded near the route during the trip window, all expressway speed bands were free-flowing (60–69 km/h), and the weather was fair with no rain; the only slow band was on Paya Lebar Road, which is not on the alternative the driver claims the GPS chose.

No consent was given for any route change: there were no in-app chat messages between rider and driver, so no rider message precedes the 12:46 segment start; the driver's own statement is a post-trip narrative about following his GPS, not an assertion of a rider-agreed route, and a driver's account cannot substitute for the rider's own consent message.

Because this is a metered RydeTAXI trip, the deviation entered the fare directly: the fare facts bill the excess 4.61 km at $1.4099/km = $6.50, and the total charged was $42.52 with distance fare $28.31 on 20.08 km.

Refund is therefore $4.08 × ($28.31 ÷ 20.08 km = $1.4099/km) = $5.75 for the unexempted segment alone; the remaining 0.52–0.53 km difference between the billed excess (4.61 km) and the segment sum (4.08 km) is map-matching/route-corridor mileage not attributable to any segment and is not claimed.

This is a repeated breach: the rider's profile records 3 route disputes already upheld against drivers in the last 90 days and the driver's profile shows 1 prior dispute with 0 upheld, so the driver's account warrants Ryde account review alongside the refund.

weaknesses: The rider's profile shows 5 disputes in 90 days (3 upheld) (F14), which the other side may use to argue the rider disputes fares habitually and to dilute the weight of this complaint.

The driver has 640 trips in 90 days, a 4.8 rating and 0 upheld route disputes (F15); the judge may treat the deviation as an isolated navigation error rather than a pattern — although our RD-6 request only asks for account review, not a finding of 'repeated' against this driver.

The driver's statement (F8) claims his GPS routed him off at Paya Lebar; no fact in the record ties the 12:46–13:07 segment to any named road, and if the judge reads the driver as having a 'reasonable cause' explanation the segment could be found exempt — though RD-4 requires traffic evidence, which F12 shows is absent.

Claim C5's $5.75 rests on the fact-table per-km rate ($1.4099, derived from F4/F6) rather than Ryde's published taxi unit rate (policy gap G10), so the exact figure could be recalculated slightly differently.
We claim only the segment's 4.08 km and not the full billed excess of 4.61 km (F4), so a smaller sum than the rider expected is requested.

claims.assertion: The trip is RydeTAXI (metered), so only the meter's distance units for any unexcused off-route segment are refundable; the total charged was $42.52 with distance $28.31 for 20.08 km at $1.4099/km and no surge (F5, F6).

The GPS track shows one off-route segment, 12:46–13:07, driving 9.70 km where the optimal route covers 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km at up to 1720 m from the optimal route; the complaint's Paya Lebar exit matches this segment (F3).

The excess distance actually billed is $6.50 (4.61 km x $1.4099/km), which exceeds the 4.08 km extra of the single off-route segment because the remaining ~0.5 km is route-corridor and map-matching movement not attributable to any segment (F3, F4, F6).
No traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window, so the driver cannot rely on the RD-4(a) reasonable-cause exemption for the Paya Lebar deviation (F12).

The only congestion evidence on the optimal route is speed band 7 (60–69 km/h) on the CTE and PIE and band 4 (30–39 km/h) on Paya Lebar Road, all better than bands 1–2, and band records alone do not excuse a segment under RD-4(b) (F9, F10, F11).
There is no in-app chat at all in this case, so the rider sent no message before the segment started that could amount to consent to a route change (F7).

The driver's only explanation is his post-trip statement that 'I followed my GPS, it took me off at Paya Lebar', which is not rider consent and which the GPS record of a 4.08 km detour defeats (F3, F8).

Because the off-route segment is unexcused, the metered overcharge falls to be refunded, but only the distance units of the unexcused segment to the exclusion of corridor/matching distance, i.e. not the full $6.50; the segment's 4.08 km x $1.4099/km = $5.75 (rounded to the cent) (F3, F4).
The driver has 640 trips in 90 days, rating 4.8, and 0 upheld disputes, so his account should not be sent for review as a repeat offender (F15).
The rider filed 5 disputes in 90 days with 3 upheld (all route), showing a pattern of route-refund claims against this driver's otherwise clean record (F14, F15).

weaknesses: The GPS facts are against me on liability: a single unexcused off-route segment adding 4.08 km, actual 20.1 km vs 15.5 km optimal, is a breach of the shortest-and-most-direct-route duty under RD-1, and the rider's complaint mirrors it (F1, F3).
My client's own statement admits the deviation and offers no justification beyond 'my GPS', which the GPS record contradicts, so I cannot defend the extra distance as a whole (F3, F8).
There is no chat record of any rider request or agreement, so any consent argument fails, and a purely verbal agreement would not count as consent (F7).

Because this is RydeTAXI, the refund is computed from the meter, so the distance penalty is real money rather than a fixed quote; the fare fact shows $6.50 excess distance billed and the fare breakdown supports the rider's arithmetic up to the segment cap (F4, F6).

points.response: Conceded as to the framework: this is a metered RydeTAXI trip and only the distance units of the unexcused segment are refundable, computed from this trip's rate of $28.31 ÷ 20.08 km = $1.4099/km with no surge (F5, F6); this matches our own C4/C5.
Conceded: the single off-route segment is 12:46–13:07, adding 4.08 km (F3), which is the deviation the rider complains of; we do not allege any second deviation.
Agreed and expressly not claimed against the driver: we claim only the 4.08 km segment extra, and the residual ~0.5 km of corridor/matching distance is excluded per RD-2 (F3, F4).

The rider's own dispute history is irrelevant to whether this segment was deviated: the GPS record independently establishes the unexcused 4.08 km off-route segment and the absence of consent, and profile facts may never decide a case (F14, F15, F3, F7).
